$description: Every tracked file has a reader (req-project-reach). tools/check-reach.mjs walks the repository from the roots below, following what a reached file names — a path, an import, a pattern in `inputs` — and requires the walk to end holding every file in the git index. This file is everything the walk cannot derive from the text: where it starts, and which trees an outside tool opens without leaving a trace inside.
$roots: Files a tool finds by its own convention, so nothing in the repository has to point at them. Two forms and no third: `path` is one file at one place, `name` is a file name a tool looks for at any depth. Neither may carry a wildcard — a pattern here would take a whole tree out of the measurement in a single line, which is the shape of the defect the gate exists for, and `check-reach.mjs` rejects it. The list is short on purpose: everything else in the repository is reached from these, and a file that needs an entry of its own is telling you nobody reads it.

roots.name: package.json
roots.reason: npm reads the root manifest by name and Nx takes the package manager from it; a project's own manifest is read the same way, by the name and the place — `libs/tokens/package.json` is what makes that directory a project at all.
npm writes it and `npm ci` reads it. Nothing in the repository names it — a lockfile is an artifact of the manifest above, not a file anyone imports.

The `skills` CLI reads it by name: `skills experimental_install` restores the vendored agent skills from the source and the digest recorded here, exactly as `npm ci` restores `node_modules` from the lockfile above. The trees themselves are not tracked (decision 0040), so this file is the whole of what the repository keeps of them — and a lockfile whose payload is ignored is reached by nobody inside, which is what a root is for.
The workspace configuration: Nx reads it by name before it knows any project exists.

roots.name: project.json
roots.reason: Nx enumerates project configurations by this name at any depth — that is how a directory becomes a project. A root per project would turn adding a library into an entry in this file, and the name form says the true thing instead: the tool looks for the name, not for the path.

roots.name: eslint.config.mjs
roots.reason: ESLint reads the flat config of the directory it lints, and `@nx/eslint/plugin` infers a `lint` target from exactly that file being there — the root one and the per-project ones alike.
The repository's front page: GitHub renders it on the landing page. It is NOT the npm page — that one is the library's own README below, and the two answer to different readers.

The npm page of `@pacit/components`. ng-packagr copies it into `dist` by its own convention — `ng-package.json` names the `themes` assets and says nothing about this file — so nothing in the repository has to point at it, and until B3 the only thing that did was the task in the plan that was going to rewrite it.
GitHub and npm find the licence by name — decision 0015 makes MIT a fact about the whole repository, so the file answers to no single project.
GitHub links it from the issue and pull request forms without anything pointing at it from inside.
The convention most agent tools read by name. It is the source of truth for the rules of this repository — `CLAUDE.md` imports it rather than the other way round.
Claude Code loads it by name and expands the `@AGENTS.md` import in it.
git reads it by name. It is also the only record of which untracked paths are deliberate — `docs/private/` and the fixtures' `dist` exception.
Editors read it by name before any project configuration.
prettier finds its configuration by name; `nx format` runs prettier and passes it nothing.
prettier finds it by name. AGENTS.md explains why the symlink it would have replaced cannot exist.
GitHub Actions enumerates `.github/workflows/`. Every gate of this repository runs from here, so the walk enters most of `tools/` through it.
The second workflow the same enumeration finds — the publication path, which runs on a tag rather than on a push.
The MCP server list, read by name by every client that supports the protocol.
Claude Code reads it by name: the Nx plugin declared here is where that tool gets the workspace skills from, instead of a copy of them in the repository.
The dev server definition the same tool reads by name when it opens a preview.
opencode reads it by name. It is also the proof that the tool is configured here at all, which is what the `.opencode` entry of the register below leans on.
VS Code reads it by name and offers the recommended extensions on opening the workspace.
The debug configurations, found by name in the same directory.

$enumerated: Trees an outside tool walks. Its reading leaves nothing inside the repository — no import, no path in a configuration — so no measurement can find the edge and an entry has to assert it. Each names the READER and stands only while it grants something: `check-reach.mjs` repeats the walk without the register and fires on an entry whose tree is reached anyway. The gates' own `check-<x>.fixtures/` trees are NOT here — that pairing follows from the names and the script derives it, so this list can never grow an entry that no gate backs.

enumerated.reason: The same assembly as the sandbox entry below, for the docs suite: Playwright composes a baseline's path from `snapshotPathTemplate` and the TEST TITLE, so the file name stands in no file. The same recorded cost too — a baseline whose test was deleted stays here unseen, and the measurement that catches it is the specs read through `playwright test --list`, not a second register.

Playwright composes a baseline's path from `snapshotPathTemplate` and the TEST TITLE, so the file name stands in no file — it is assembled at runtime from a sentence. What this entry costs is written down rather than hidden: a baseline whose test was deleted stays here and this gate will not say so, because it never looked inside the tree. Catching that needs the measurement `check-browsers` already does — the specs read through `playwright test --list` — and not a second register.

opencode walks its own directory: skills, agents and commands are found by the shape of the tree, and the name of a skill is what AGENTS.md tells an agent to invoke — never a path. The tracked configuration next to it is the proof the tool is in use here; the copy of the same tree for a tool that is NOT configured here was what B9 deleted.
